Hugging Face and its Pollen Robotics subsidiary have opened preorders for Microduck, a $399 desktop-sized robot built for experimenting with “physical AI.”  The 25cm robot contains 15 motors, a camera, a depth sensor, two inertial measurement units, and a “beak” that can grasp small objects.  Its open-source software allows developers to train behaviors through reinforcement learning in a physics simulator before transferring them to the real machine.  Microduck can already walk, crouch, follow a laser, grab objects, and recover from many falls.  More than 10,000 units were preordered in its first five days, roughly $4 million! Initial deliveries are targeted before Christmas of this year in North America, Europe, and the UK. Would you buy one?

iRobot co-founder Colin Angle, whose company sold over 50 million Roombas, has unveiled his new venture, Familiar Machines & Magic. Its first product is a furry, bear-like quadruped robot with 23 motorized joints, a touch-sensitive coat, cameras, and microphones. The robot communicates through expressive movements rather than speech. A custom onboard AI gives it personality and memory while keeping user data off the cloud. Beyond companionship, it aims to reinforce healthy routines, like limiting screen time. Angle compares its cost to pet ownership, targeting sales next year. Whether it can sustain long-term engagement, where past social robots failed, remains the big question.

I spent days teaching a 3D-printed robot duck to walk. Most of that time, it was falling over. It’s my own build of the Open Duck Mini. The open-source, BDX-inspired biped created by Antoine Pirrone. The whole thing is 3D-printed and runs on hobby-grade servos instead of industrial actuators, which is what makes it buildable on a normal budget and also what makes it so hard to get walking. The hard part wasn’t the printing or the assembly. It was the sim-to-real gap. A gait that walks perfectly in MuJoCo hits real-world joint slop, servo lag, and a center of mass that won’t sit still, and just before you know it, the duck face plants into the floor. It took me 40+ calibration passes before it could take three steps without tipping! What the build came down to: • 3D-printed chassis • Per-joint offset calibration (where most of the pain lived) • Policy training in simulation (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) • Build guide + docs via Tnkr • A lot of failed walks Real hardware. Real failures. Real progress.

This piece is going to become a robot, although right now it is still at the stage where the structure does most of the talking. The armature is made from thick wire, fixed onto a wooden base, and the surface is starting to take shape with epoxy putty and found objects, including fragments of toys and other small elements. It is a process of building from whatever works best, combining sculptural modelling with materials that already carry their own strange character. One of the most useful tricks in this kind of work is surprisingly simple: cut plastic spoons. For @tomasbarcelocastela, they are a practical way to create large, smooth, geometric forms very quickly. They can be trimmed into different shapes and used as a base to establish these clean volumes before continuing to model over the top. For now it is still simple, large and geometric, but the sculpture is already beginning to find its identity. #TomasBarcelo #Sculpture #RobotSculpture #ContemporarySculpture #MixedMediaArt #MixedMediaSculpture #EpoxySculpture #EpoxyPutty #FoundObjects #AssemblageArt #SculptureProcess #WorkInProgress #BehindTheScenes #ArtistStudio #StudioPractice #CreativeProcess #GeometricSculpture #WireArmature #HandmadeArt #ObjectArt #RecycledArt #UpcycledArt #FigurativeSculpture #ArtProcess #Sculptor #SpanishSculptor #ContemporaryArt
